templates.source_problem: Find where the normal line to the curve $f(x)=2{x}^{2}+x$ at the point $(1,3)$ intersects the $x$-axis.
templates.source_solution:
Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{2}+x)=4x+1.\end{aligned}
$$

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m={f}^{′}(1)=4(1)+1=5,
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{5}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-3 & =-\frac{1}{5}(x-1) \\ y & =-\frac{1}{5}x+\frac{1}{5}+3 \\ y & =-\frac{1}{5}x+\frac{16}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $x$-axis by setting $y=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{5}x+\frac{16}{5} & =0 \\ x & =16.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal line intersects the $x$-axis at $(16,0).$

templates.source_problem: Find where the normal line to the curve $f(x)=2\sqrt{x}$ at the point $(1,2)$ intersects the $y$-axis.
templates.source_solution:
Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2\sqrt{x}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{1/2}) \\  & ={x}^{-1/2} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m={f}^{′}(1)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1}}=1,
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-1.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-2 & =-1(x-1) \\ y & =-x+1+2 \\ y & =-x+3.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $y$-axis by setting $x=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-0+3 \\ y & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal line intersects the $y$-axis at  $(0,3).$

templates.source_solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{'}(x)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})=2x.\end{aligned}
$$

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m={f}^{'}(3)=2(3)=6,
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

$$
{m}^{'}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{6}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-9 & =-\frac{1}{6}(x-3) \\ y & =-\frac{1}{6}x+\frac{1}{2}+9 \\ y & =-\frac{1}{6}x+\frac{19}{2}.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{6}x+\frac{19}{2} & =0 \\ \frac{19}{2} & =\frac{1}{6}x \\ x & =57.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal line intersects the $x$-axis at $(57,0).$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}-2x+4 & =0 \\ 2x & =4 \\ x & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal line intersects the $x$-axis at $(\,2,0\,).$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3\sqrt[3]{{x}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3{x}^{2/3}) \\  & =2{x}^{-1/3} \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt[3]{x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m={f}^{′}(8)=\frac{2}{\sqrt[3]{8}}=1,
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-1.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-12 & =-(x-8) \\ y & =-x+8+12 \\ y & =20-x.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $y$-axis by setting $x=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =20-0 \\ y & =20.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal line intersects the $y$-axis at  $(0,20).$

$$

{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=\frac{1}{2}.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{5}{2} & =0 \\ x & =-5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal line intersects the  $x$-axis at $(\,-5,0\,).$
